spots.name: Lincoln Road
spots.label: Lincoln Road

text.geographic_location: Lincoln Road is in South Beach, in the southern part of Miami Beach. The mall runs between 16th Street and 17th Street, from Washington Avenue in the east to Alton Road in the west.
text.access_note: Lincoln Road Mall is a public pedestrian street, but check the official site before you go if you plan to photograph inside a venue or at an event.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Lincoln Road area of South Beach and head for the pedestrian mall between 16th and 17th Street. Just walk along the street; it is car-free. The phone icon on the map is about 210 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description:
Lincoln Road is the pedestrian shopping street of South Beach, a long, car-free mall running east to west between 16th Street and 17th Street. It was a mangrove forest until 1912, when Carl Fisher cleared a strip across the island from the ocean side to Biscayne Bay. In the 1950s the architect Morris Lapidus redesigned it in his Miami Modern ("MiMo") style, with gardens, fountains, shelters and an amphitheatre. It had its grand opening as a pedestrian mall on 28 November 1960, and it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.

For photos, the mall gives you a long straight view with cafe tables, palms, shop fronts and people strolling, so the scene has plenty of depth. Street performers and the mix of old and new buildings add variety, and the Lapidus shapes and planted areas make good foreground detail. Walk a little further to find the garden-style western block by Raymond Jungles, a good place for greenery shots. It is a busy place, so allow time to wait for a gap in the crowd, and watch your bag and phone when you stop to compose.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 210 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street as you see it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full width of the mall with tables and palms. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a performer, a shop front or a detail of the planting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the quietest time for clear views of the street. In the late afternoon and evening the mall is livelier and the lights come on, but you will be facing west, towards the low sun, so use the exposure slider.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the street or a person to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is washing out. If a stranger is clearly the subject, try portrait mode; otherwise stay with the normal photo mode. After dark, night mode helps with the shop and restaurant lights, but hold the phone against something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up with the centre so the shop fronts lead the eye down the mall. Keep your phone level, as tilting will bend the vertical lines of the buildings. Put some tables or planters in the foreground for depth, and wait for a gap in the crowd if you want a clear view. For a closer shot, try a side-on view of a garden or fountain area.

spots.name: Fontainebleau Miami Beach
spots.label: Fontainebleau

text.geographic_location: The Fontainebleau sits on Collins Avenue in Miami Beach, Florida, on the oceanfront side of the avenue.
text.access_note: Collins Avenue is a public street, but the hotel and its Ocean Lawn are private property where you may be asked to move on, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed for this spot, so head for Collins Avenue in Miami Beach by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Fontainebleau. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.description: The Fontainebleau is one of Miami Beach's best-known mid-century hotels, designed by Morris Lapidus and opened in 1954. Its big curved oceanfront wing is the shape everyone remembers, and it is the reason the hotel works so well in a photo. From Collins Avenue you can line the curve up down the street, and it looks best when the building is lit at dusk or after dark. The hotel has a long film history too. It appears in the opening aerial shot after the credits of the 1964 James Bond film Goldfinger. Its architecture has also been recognised: in 2012 the American Institute of Architects' Florida Chapter ranked it first on its list of Florida's 100 places, and it joined the National Register of Historic Places in December 2008. That was the same year it reopened after a renovation of about $1 billion, which added newer towers while keeping Lapidus's original look. For a phone photo, stand on the pavement of Collins Avenue and look north, so the curved front sits to your right and leads the eye down the avenue. Keep the vertical lines straight with the gridlines. Wait for the lights to come on rather than shooting in flat daylight. An alternative is the hotel's Ocean Lawn on the oceanfront side, which gives sunrise light with the Atlantic in front, but it is hotel property.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Collins Avenue (looking north along Collins Avenue toward the curved oceanfront facade). The hotel's curved Lapidus facade framed down the avenue, most striking when the building is lit at night. The hotel's long curved oceanfront front is to the east, on your right, and should lead into the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the curved facade down the avenue. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the street and sky, but keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can stretch. The telephoto (2x or more) is useful for picking out the curve of the front from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Night, at blue hour, when the facade is lit and the sky still has some colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use night mode once the light drops, and hold the phone steady with your elbows tucked in. Tap on the lit facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights do not wash out. Take a few shots, as passing traffic will change each one.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the avenue's edge as a guide line, keeping the building's verticals upright. Leave some dark sky above the roofline. If you have time at the Ocean Lawn on the oceanfront side, it gives a different view of the building with the sea and sunrise in front, but it is hotel property, so check the official site before you go.

spots.alt: Fontainebleau Miami Beach, Miami Beach: one of Miami Beach's best-known mid-century hotels. Photo spot

spots.name: Ocean Drive
spots.label: Ocean Drive

text.geographic_location: Ocean Drive is in the South Beach district at the southern end of Miami Beach. It runs from South Pointe to 15th Street, starting about a quarter mile west of the Atlantic at its southern end, and lies just south-east of Lincoln Road.
text.access_note: Ocean Drive is a public street with hotels, bars and restaurants along it; cars were banned during 2020 to 2022 but it has since reopened to traffic, so check the official site before you go for any current changes.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. From it, the subject point is about 6 to 7 minutes on foot to the south along the street. The phone icon on the map is about 510 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.description: Ocean Drive is a major street in South Beach, the southern part of Miami Beach. It runs north from South Pointe, just south of 1st Street, up to 15th Street, close to the Atlantic. It sits at the centre of the Miami Art Deco District, which has about 900 preserved buildings and is on the National Register of Historic Places. The street was developed in the 1920s and 1930s, and the rounded Streamline Moderne style dominates it. That is what you are photographing: rows of pastel hotel fronts, curved corners, neon signs and café terraces, all lined up along one straight street. The 1939 Colony Hotel is described as the most photographed Art Deco hotel here, and it makes an easy anchor for a picture. The Carlyle appeared in The Birdcage (1996), and the Clevelander is another popular Art Deco hotel. The street is long, so pick one stretch and keep your picture simple. A wide shot down the pavement shows the whole line of buildings, while a closer shot of a single sign, balcony or doorway shows the detail. Pavements and terraces get busy, so look for gaps between people or include them for a sense of life.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 510 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. From there the line of Art Deco buildings leads your eye down the road. Walk south for closer pictures of individual hotels.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most street views. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want a whole hotel front, or when you are close to a building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a sign or rooftop detail further down the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, with softer light on the facades. Around dusk and after dark the neon signs come on and the street looks quite different.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a pastel wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the colours stay rich and neon signs do not blow out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against something firm to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the buildings straight. Place the street along a diagonal to give the picture depth. For a single hotel, stand square-on to the front and use the 1x lens. For a more relaxed street scene, include a few pedestrians or café tables for scale.
